steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Fate (fatum) is the driving force of the Aeneid: Aeneas's destiny to found Rome is decreed by Jupiter and cannot be avoided.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Pietas (duty to gods, country, and family) is Aeneas's defining quality: he is called 'pius Aeneas' throughout the epic. But pietas demands terrible personal sacrifices.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Love and loss: Dido's love for Aeneas and her suicide is the Aeneid's most tragic episode, showing how fate destroys personal happiness.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Power and transformation in Ovid: the gods use power to pursue desire, and transformation is both punishment and escape.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always support theme discussion with specific Latin quotations — themes without textual evidence earn minimal marks. When discussing a theme, consider how it develops across the prescribed passages rather than in isolation. Use the Latin terms: fatum, pietas, furor, ratio — they show precise understanding. For the Aeneid, be ready to discuss the ambivalence of themes: pietas is noble but also destructive; fate brings glory but also suffering.
